title: Effects of enteric‐coated, low‐dose aspirin on parameters of platelet function

sections.abstract: <jats:title>SUMMARY</jats:title><jats:p><jats:bold>Background</jats:bold> : Aspirin is widely used as an anti‐thrombotic drug; however, it has been suggested that enteric‐coated formulations of aspirin may be less bioavailable and less effective as anti‐thrombotic agents.</jats:p><jats:p><jats:bold>Aim</jats:bold> : To assess the effect of a formulation of enteric‐coated, low‐dose (81 mg) aspirin on serum generated thromboxane B<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> and platelet aggregation in healthy subjects.</jats:p><jats:p><jats:bold>Methods</jats:bold> : Twenty‐four subjects participated in a double‐blind, randomized, placebo‐controlled, parallel‐group, multiple‐dose study. Twelve subjects in each of two groups received a daily oral dose of enteric‐coated aspirin (81 mg) or matching placebo for 7 days. Serum thromboxane B<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> and platelet aggregation (using 1 m<jats:sc>m</jats:sc> arachidonic acid and 1 µg/mL collagen as agonists) were measured 1–3 days prior to day 1, on day 1 (prior to therapy) and 4 h after the last dose on day 7.</jats:p><jats:p><jats:bold>Results</jats:bold> : After seven daily doses of enteric‐coated aspirin, the mean percentage inhibition from baseline of <jats:italic>ex vivo</jats:italic> generated serum thromboxane B<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> was 97.4%, compared with a 7.8% increase after placebo treatment. The mean percentage inhibition of arachidonic acid‐ and collagen‐induced platelet aggregation was 97.9% and 70.9%, respectively, following enteric‐coated aspirin, compared with − 1.0% and 2.7%, respectively, after placebo.</jats:p><jats:p><jats:bold>Conclusions</jats:bold> : The anti‐platelet effects of multiple, daily, low‐dose aspirin (as assessed by inhibition of serum thromboxane B<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> and platelet aggregation) are not adversely affected by enteric coating.</jats:p>
